blocks.html: A memory palace hangs items on places. A peg system hangs them on numbers. You learn, once, a picture for each number. Then any list can be hung on those pictures.
A peg is fixed (the same every time) and easy to picture. Item 3 goes with peg 3, so you can answer "What was third?" right away.
A palace needs you to walk to spot 7. A peg lets you jump straight to 7. Pegs are good for short numbered lists; palaces handle long ones.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Your peg for 4 is a door. Item 4 on your list is a kite. Make the link.
steps: Vivid link: a kite crashes through the door and gets stuck, tail flapping.
blocks.a: A kite stuck in the door.

blocks.html: Reusing the same pegs for a new list the same day. Old images can linger and mix in; give the old list time to fade or use another set.
The oldest and easiest pegs rhyme with their numbers. This is a common list; you may change a peg if another rhyme is easier for you to picture, but then keep it.
Say the number, hear the rhyme, see the picture. Then link the item to the picture.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Hang a short list on the rhyme pegs: 1 milk, 2 stamps, 3 batteries.
steps: 1 bun: a bun soaking in a puddle of milk.
2 shoe: a shoe covered in stamps.
3 tree: a tree with batteries hanging like fruit.

blocks.html: Rhyme makes the peg come back with no effort, which is what a peg must do.
Some people find it easier to see a number than to hear a rhyme. Number-shape pegs use what each digit looks like. Here is one common set; pick your own if another shape is clearer to you.

head: Digit
Peg
Why
rows: a curve hanging from a bar
a curved head at the bottom

blocks.html: Look at the digit, see its object, then link the item to that object.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Use shape pegs: item 8 is a trumpet.
steps: Link: a snowman playing a trumpet so loudly his carrot nose falls off.

blocks.html: Once your pegs are solid, a ten-item list takes only a few minutes to hang.
One item per peg. To recall item 6, go straight to peg 6. To recall the whole list, run through the pegs in order.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: You hung these on the rhyme pegs: 1 bun-map, 2 shoe-lamp, 3 tree-violin, 4 door-pizza, 5 hive-rope. What was item 4? What came after the lamp?
steps: Peg 4 is door; the door held pizza.
The lamp was on peg 2; peg 3, tree, held the violin.

blocks.html: Ten pegs cover ten items. For longer lists, use a journey (later in this course) or a bigger peg list such as the Major System's 00 to 99.

Pegs from rhymes and shapes stop at 10. The Major System goes much further. It turns digits into consonant sounds, and sounds can be joined with vowels into words: any number can become a word or a picture.

Its roots go back to the 1600s; the French teacher Aimé Paris gave it much of its modern form in 1825, and it was spread in English in the 1800s. Many memory athletes build their number systems on it today.

head: Digit
Sounds
A hook to learn it
rows: r is the last sound of four
a J turned around looks like 6
a K is two 7s back to back
a cursive f has two loops, like 8
p is a mirror image of 9

blocks.html: Each digit is a sound. Vowel sounds (a, e, i, o, u) and the sounds of w, h and y count as nothing, so you can use them freely to make words.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: What number does "mat" make?

blocks.title: The other way
blocks.q: Turn 92 into sounds and then a word.
steps: Add vowels: b + o + n + e makes "bone."

blocks.html: Thinking each letter is a digit. In "hat" the h is free, so hat is 1, not two digits.

sources.name: College Info Geek: Major mnemonic system reference (the sound table)

blocks.html: The Major System listens; it doesn't read. Four rules cover almost every case.

items: Silent letters count for nothing. knife: n, f = 28. lamb: l, m = 53.
A double letter that makes one sound is one digit. hammer: m, r = 34. bell: b, l = 95.
c and g follow their sound. cat (hard c, k) = 71; city (soft c, s) = 01; goat (hard g) = 71; giraffe (soft g, j) = 648.
x is two sounds, k and s: box = 970. ph sounds like f: phone = 82.

blocks.html: Say the word aloud. Write down only the consonant sounds you hear, then turn each into its digit.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Code "chef."

blocks.title: Double letters
blocks.q: Code "kitten."
steps: Sounds: k, t, n (the tt is one sound).

blocks.html: Coding the "ng" in "ring" without thinking. Systems differ on ng, so it is best to avoid ng words in your list.

sources.name: College Info Geek: Major mnemonic system reference (the sound table)

blocks.html: The first step in remembering a number is turning its digits into sounds.
One digit, one consonant sound, in order. Then add vowels to find a word.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Turn 4,175 into sounds.
blocks.a: r · t · k · l (for example, "r d k l").

blocks.title: Making a word
blocks.q: Find a word for 21.
steps: Add vowels: n + e + t = net; n + u + t = nut.

head: Pair to watch
Sounds
rows: 6 is the soft j, sh, ch; 7 is the hard k, g
8 is f, v (lips and teeth); 9 is p, b (both lips)
0 is s, z (hiss); 1 is t, d (tap)

sources.name: College Info Geek: Major mnemonic system reference (the sound table)

blocks.html: Decoding is how you get the number back out. You see the image (a goat), say the word, and read the sounds.
Say the word. Keep consonant sounds only. Drop vowels and w, h, y. Change each sound to its digit.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Decode "rocket."
steps: Sounds: r, k, t (the ck is one k sound).

blocks.title: Free letters
blocks.q: Decode "honey."
steps: h is free; n = 2; y is free.

blocks.title: Silent letters
blocks.q: Decode "lighthouse."

sources.name: College Info Geek: Major mnemonic system reference (the sound table)

blocks.html: Making a word on the spot is slow. So most people who use the Major System choose one picture word for each number from 00 to 99 and learn it until it is instant. Then 1492 is not four digits to code; it is two pictures.
Here is a list we wrote for this course. Every word was checked against its sounds. Choose your own if another word is easier to picture, but keep each one fixed.
Read the row for the first digit and the column for the second: 47 is row 4_, column 7: rock.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Which words stand for 1492?
blocks.a: Tire, bone: a tire rolling over a bone.

blocks.html: A fixed list turns every two digits into one picture, so a number half as many images. Twenty digits become ten pictures.

sources.name: College Info Geek: Major mnemonic system reference (the sound table)

blocks.html: To learn a long number, combine two tools: the Major System to turn digits into pictures, and a journey to keep the pictures in order.

items: Split the number into pairs (a final single digit uses a one-digit word).
Turn each pair into its list word.
Put one or two pictures at each spot on your route.
To recall, walk the route and decode.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Learn 31415926 (the first eight digits of pi).
steps: Route: front door (a mat), stairs (a rat), mirror (lips), sofa (a notch cut in it).

blocks.html: Pictures needed = digits ÷ 2, rounded up. Stops needed = pictures ÷ pictures per stop, rounded up.

blocks.title: Counting stops
blocks.q: A 30-digit number with 2 pictures per stop. How many stops?

blocks.html: Dates are a natural job for the Major System. A four-digit year is two list words. Join them in one picture with the event.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: The Declaration of Independence was adopted in 1776.
steps: Picture: a duck in a cage signing a huge scroll with a feather quill.

blocks.title: Another
blocks.q: Magna Carta was sealed in 1215.
steps: Picture: a tuna using its tail to press a wax seal onto a long charter.

blocks.html: Event + two pictures in one scene. Many people drop the leading 1 or 19 when the century is obvious and code only the last two digits.
Coding 1215 as "12" and "15" without the event. The picture must include the charter, or you will know a date but not what happened.
A deck of cards is 52 items in a random order: a classic memory challenge. The first step is a code: a fixed image for every card.

Many people build card codes from the Major System. One common way: the suit gives a first sound and the value gives a second, so each card becomes a word. Others simply pick a person for each card. Either works if it is fixed and well learned.
52 cards need 52 images. Learn them as a peg list before you try a deck.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: A deck is 4 suits of 13 values. How many codes do you need?

blocks.html: The site's deck-of-cards challenge lets you practice with a shuffled deck: Memory challenges.
PAO stands for person, action, object. For every card you choose a person, something that person typically does, and an object they use.
For three cards in a row: the person from the first card, the action from the second, the object from the third. One picture, three cards.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: The cards come up A♠, 7♦, K♥. What is the picture?

blocks.html: Three cards per picture means a deck of 52 needs only 18 pictures (17 groups of three, and one left over), so a journey with 18 stops holds it.
Building a story across pictures. Each PAO picture sits on its own spot; the route does the ordering.
Before a run, memory athletes know exactly how many stops they need. The arithmetic is short.
Pictures = items ÷ items per picture (round up). Stops = pictures ÷ pictures per stop (round up).

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: A deck in PAO, with 2 pictures on each stop. How many stops?

blocks.title: Per stop
blocks.q: How many cards does one stop hold with PAO and 2 pictures per stop?

blocks.html: For long lists you need many stops. A journey links several rooms, or a walk through a town, into one long route.

items: Plan the route on paper first: house, then the street, then the school...
Mark every fifth stop with something special, like a mailbox, so you always know where you are.
Walk it in your head, forward and backward, before you use it.
Use the same direction every time.

blocks.html: A journey is only useful once it is automatic. Learn the route like a peg list before you hang anything on it.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: You need 40 stops. Your house gives 15. What next?
steps: Add routes you know: the yard and the walk to the park.
Join them in a fixed order.
blocks.a: Extend the route outdoors until you have 40.

blocks.html: Because every stop has a fixed place in the order, a journey can answer "What is at stop 12?" or "What came before the rope?"

items: rope
lamp
drum
kite
bell
boat

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Walk: gate (rope), porch (lamp), door (drum), hall (kite), kitchen (bell), garden (boat). What came just before the bell?
steps: The bell is at the kitchen, stop 5.
Stop 4 is the hall, which holds the kite.

blocks.html: Count stops in a fixed direction. Every fifth stop is a landmark that keeps the count honest.
Capacity is simple arithmetic, and it saves surprises.
Holds = stops × pictures per stop × items per picture. Needs = items ÷ (pictures per stop × items per picture), rounded up.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: A palace with 20 stops, 2 pictures per stop, 2 digits per picture. How many digits does it hold?

blocks.title: Stops needed
blocks.q: You need to memorize 100 digits with 2 digits per picture and 1 picture per stop. How many stops?

blocks.html: If you put a new list on a route the same day as an old one, the old images may still be there. People call these leftovers ghosts.

items: For lists you want to keep for good (the presidents), give them their own route and leave it alone.
For practice and one-time lists, rotate several routes, and give each one a day or two to clear.
Make new images extra vivid so they outshine any ghost.

blocks.html: Keep permanent lists on their own routes. Rotate practice routes.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: You practice a deck every day with one route. Images from yesterday keep showing up. What helps?
steps: Give each a rest before you use it again.

blocks.html: The link method needs no places. Picture item 1 and item 2 together, then item 2 and item 3, and so on, like a chain.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Link: dog, umbrella, piano, cake.
steps: Dog and umbrella: a dog walking on two legs under a tiny umbrella.
Umbrella and piano: an umbrella opens out of a piano and plays a tune.
Piano and cake: a piano made of cake, frosting on the keys.

blocks.html: Each picture holds two items: the one you have and the next one.
Links are quick to make, which is why they suit short lists. But if one link fails, everything after it is lost. A journey is safer for long lists.
The story method is the link method with a plot. Instead of separate pairs, one story moves from item to item.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Story for: frog, ladder, cloud, spoon, bell.
steps: A frog climbs a ladder up into a cloud.
The spoons clang on a bell, and everyone wakes up.

blocks.html: Each item causes the next: "so," "and then," "because." Keep the story short and test the list, not the story.
Remembering the story but not the items in order. After telling it, list the items alone.

sources.name: Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)

head: The job
A good fit
rows: A short list, under about ten items
Card codes or PAO on a journey
A journey, one point per stop

blocks.html: The systems combine: Major words placed on a journey is how most long numbers are learned.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: You must recall item 37 of a 50-item list on request. Which fits best?
steps: You need jump-to access by number and a long list.
A journey with every fifth stop marked, or a 00 to 99 peg list.
blocks.a: A numbered journey or Major pegs.

blocks.html: When you need exact words, such as a poem, a passage or a pledge, try first-letter cues. Write only the first letter of each word, then recite from the letters.
Robert Frost, "Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening" (1923):

Whose woods these are I think I know.
His house is in the village though;
He will not see me stopping here
To watch his woods fill up with snow.
First letters: W w t a I t I k. / H h i i t v t; / H w n s m s h / T w h w f u w s.
Cue card = first letters + the punctuation. It gives just enough to recall, but not enough to read.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Make the cue for "Twinkle, twinkle, little star."
steps: Twinkle T, twinkle t, little l, star s.

blocks.html: First letters turn reading into recall, which is what makes a memory stick.
A good way to learn verse is cumulative: each new line joins the lines before it.
Say from the start each round. The joins between lines get the most practice.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: A stanza has 4 lines. With cumulative rounds, how many lines will you say in all?

blocks.html: Then space the stanza: recite it on days 1, 3, 7 and 21. Add a new stanza only when the old one is solid.

sources.name: Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)

blocks.html: Ancient orators used memory palaces to give long speeches without notes: one point at each place.

items: Write the speech, then reduce it to its key points.
Put one point at each stop of a journey, as a vivid picture.
Learn the first and last lines word for word, for a strong start and finish.
Practice aloud, walking the route; let the wording in between change a little.

blocks.html: Order comes from the route; the words come from understanding.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: A talk has 6 points. How many stops do you need?
blocks.a: 6 stops (plus the opening and closing, if you like).

blocks.html: To practice exact wording, the Gettysburg Address (1863) is short and public: "Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent, a new nation, conceived in Liberty, and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal."
Memory competitions have run since the 1990s. Events include memorizing a shuffled deck as fast as possible, long numbers, binary digits, random words, names and faces, and historic dates.
Competitors use the same tools you are learning: journeys, the Major System, PAO and steady practice.

Researchers who have studied top memory athletes found that nearly all of them use the method of loci. In the 2017 study in the next topic, the athletes' brains did not differ in structure from other people's; the difference was in how brain regions worked together, which fits a learned skill.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Why do memory athletes practice with a timer?
steps: Speed comes from codes becoming instant.
blocks.a: Their events are timed, and speed shows when codes are automatic.

sources.name: Dresler, M., and others (2017). Mnemonic training reshapes brain networks to support superior memory. Neuron 93(5)

blocks.html: In 2017, Martin Dresler and colleagues published a study in the journal Neuron. They compared 23 memory athletes with ordinary people, then trained 51 adults with no memory training before.

head: Group
What they did for 40 days
Words recalled (of 72)
rows: 30 minutes a day of memory palace practice

blocks.html: Four months later, with no more training, the loci group still recalled over 22 words more than at the start. Brain scans showed their connections shifting toward the pattern seen in the memory athletes.
Training the method of loci produced large, lasting gains in remembering lists. It is a trained skill, open to ordinary people.
Overstating it. The study measured word-list recall, not school grades or general intelligence. The skill helps most with what you practice it on.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Before training, the loci group recalled about 26 words; after, about 62. How many more?
blocks.a: About 36 more words (the paper reports about 35).

sources.name: Dresler, M., and others (2017). Mnemonic training reshapes brain networks to support superior memory. Neuron 93(5)
ScienceDaily (2017). Memory athletes: Super-sized memory is trainable and long lasting (a summary of Dresler and others)

blocks.html: If you want to try memory challenges, here is a plan that matches what works.

items: Weeks 1 to 2: learn your 00 to 99 list or card codes as flashcards, with spaced review.
Weeks 3 to 4: build and walk three or more journeys.
Then: short daily drills, 15 to 30 minutes, on one event. Accuracy first.
Log your time and errors. Fix the codes that cause errors.
Keep permanent lists on their own routes with the 1-3-7-21 schedule.
Sleep well, and keep it fun.

blocks.html: Codes first, then routes, then speed. Short and daily beats long and rare.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Ty can memorize 20 cards in 3 minutes with 4 errors. What should he work on?
steps: Find which codes caused the errors and drill them.
blocks.a: The codes behind his errors, before trying to go faster.

blocks.html: Try your skills on the challenges and games.
